http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/02/at-le.text: At least five people have died and 41 are still missing after an Indonesian ferry caught fire at sea, on Sunday. According according to Basarnas, Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency some passengers jumped overboard to escape the fire and were rescued by a nearby ship.Meanwhile, a total of 225 people onboard were rescued, and four other boats were on standby near the ferry, however they could not get close due to the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, said the regional Surabaya Search and Rescue Agency.The ferry company had received a call from the ship's captain to report the fire as it sailed from Surabaya in East Java to Makassar in South Sulawesi.However, Basarnas said the captain had not been in contact after that, adding that a larger rescue operation was on its way from Surabaya, a six-hour journey from the site of the disaster.Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Ministry of Transportation said in a statement: "Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site."Adding, "the safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively".Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, experiences marine accidents frequently, in some parts due to a lack of following of the safety standards and unpredictable weather.Last month at least four people died and 14 remained missing until search and rescue operations concluded after a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near the small tropical island of Selayar south of the much larger Sulawesi.

Zach Cregger gives update on Aunt Gladys prequel, reveals the ‘Weapons’ scene that made him cry Marcus Errico Share on Facebook Post Google Preferred Pin it Show more sharing options Share to Flipboard Post to Tumblr Submit to Reddit Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Email Print This Page Zach Cregger was one of the featured attractions at the "Directors on Directing" panel at Comic-Con International on Thursday. The session, which also featured the Dungeons & Dragons and Game Night duo of Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley, allowed Cregger to take a much-deserved but long-delayed victory lap for Weapons . It also afforded an opportunity to tease the upcoming Aunt Gladys prequel , which will fill in the backstory of the character that earned Amy Madigan her Oscar. Here are the highlights: On the status of the Aunt Gladys movie Zach Cregger: I'm really excited about the Gladys movie. I loved working with Amy, I love that character, and for Weapons it made a lot of sense not to dive into her backstory, because the device of the film was to keep her very opaque and mysterious. However, there's an amazing story to be told about where Gladys comes from and how she became what we know her as. It's got a lot of twists and turns and mysteries, kind of like Weapons does, and I think it's going to be great. The script is in process now. We're taking it super seriously, and it's moving in the right direction. It's been written — that's the short answer. Related Stories ‘Sinners,’ ‘One Battle After Another,’ and ‘Weapons’ lead MacGuffin Awards nominations Why ‘Widow’s Bay’ may be this year’s Emmys dark horse The timetable for the Gladys prequel Cregger: My next project is going to be a science-fiction movie called Flood that I wrote. After Barbarian , I wrote Weapons , Flood , and Resident Evil in the same blast. I had a year-and-a-half hiatus between Barbarian and starting Weapons — I didn't know which movie was going to go — and it ended up being Weapons , then Resident Evil , and then Flood will be next. After that, we'll see. The best advice he got while making Weapons Cregger: When I was doing Weapons , I was very fortunate to be able to show the movie to David Fincher and have him sit with me and talk about a lot of different scenes. One lesson I learned from him was: first, stabilize everything. Don't shoot in anamorphic handheld — stabilize. I learned that the hard way. Another was about audio. There's a scene in Weapons where he blew my mind: Julia Garner is getting out of the car and walking from the car to her house, and we're focused on her. She looks to her left, and we rack focus down the block, because she's worried someone's going to attack her, and then we rack back to her and follow her to the house. Dave's idea was: rack the audio, don't just rack the visual. So we had all these cicadas in the street, and when we racked to the distance, we dropped down a certain frequency of cicadas and turned up a distant reverb — a slightly different tone of cicada — and suddenly it had this incredible effect of making me feel like I was really there. Such a simple tool. It taught me that you're never done. When you're in the edit, there's always more to explore, and there are so many more tools at your disposal than I was even letting myself think about. The lesson was: take every scene you think you're done with, and just keep going — keep pushing, keep exploring. His favorite scene from Weapons Cregger: For me, there was a moment when I was shooting Weapons . There was a scene with Amy Madigan sitting across the dining-room table from little Cary Christopher — the parents are stabbing themselves in the face — and Amy basically has a little monologue where she threatens him. It's a really simple thing: a locked-off shot on a long lens, on her face. Watching Amy take what I'd written and elevate it to such an amazing degree — I remember I was tearing up, sitting there watching her on the monitor, thinking, "This is so much better than I could have hoped." That was a moment of immense pride for me. So, that's the shot. The moment he knew Weapons was a hit Cregger: Oh my God, I don't know. When Weapons came out, I was already in Prague in the middle of making Resident Evil , so I just wasn't around for the party. I was getting some nice texts from people, but when you're in the throes of making a movie, you have one gigantic emergency after another right in front of your face. So I sort of had to skip the whole thing. It felt like watching people have a good time on the other side of a giant gap. That realization crept in over time, after it happened. By the time I came back to America, the fanfare had subsided, and I was like, "Anybody?" So — terrible answer to your question. There was no moment. Was there a favorite deleted scene? Cregger: I cut some scenes out of Weapons , but they needed to go — they just didn't move the story, so it was painless. It was like, "Oh, that didn't serve what I thought it was going to do. Out." I wish I'd cut them before I shot them. Which director on which film would he have loved to shadow Cregger: That's such a good question — I'm going to come up with a better answer as soon as I leave. But what comes to mind is probably Stanley Kubrick — any movie, but maybe Barry Lyndon , just to see him tackle something that feels so daunting to make. And not just because he makes amazing things — the more I read about him, the more I realize how bizarre his process seems by the standards we've all entrenched ourselves in. Such a different way of working and thinking. I'd just love to be there. It'd be a pleasure. By providing your information, you agree to our Terms of Use and our Privacy Policy . https://www.asiaone.com/world/drone-sink.text: world Drone sinks ship off Bulgaria, as fears grow about hybrid attacks by Russia Crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack disembark from a Bulgarian border police vessel in Varna, Bulgaria, following a rescue operation after one vessel was sunk and another damaged in the Black Sea off Bulgaria, Oct 6. PHOTO: Reuters PUBLISHED ON October 07, 2026 2:12 AM SOFIA — The crew of a merchant ship was missing on Tuesday (Oct 6) after the vessel sank in the Black Sea off NATO member Bulgaria following a drone strike that Prime Minister Rumen Radev described as a gross violation of international law. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack by air and sea drones about 130 km off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, but there are growing concerns about hybrid attacks by Russia as it wages war in Ukraine. Shipping sources said it appeared to be the first such attack in the waters of Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. Radev said it was unclear whether the drones came from Russia or from Ukraine, the BTA news agency reported. Bulgaria does not border either country but it holds a strategic position in the Black Sea, where both Ukraine and Russia have major ports. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, speaking in his nightly video address, said an investigation jointly with Bulgaria's navy showed that Russia was behind the attack. "The Ukrainian Defence Forces were conducting no operations in this part of the sea," he said. "This latest tragedy involving civilian ships is a continuation of Russia's attempt to make the western part of the Black Sea completely unsafe for navigation ... Our navy contacted their colleagues in Bulgaria and established that this was a Russian combined attack using both sea and aerial drones. Moscow has made no comment on the incident. Two ships were hit in the attack, Radev said in a televised statement. The crew of one, which was carrying grain, was rescued, with two injured. The other, which sank, was a Togo-flagged ship whose cargo was not disclosed. It is unclear how many people were on board. The incident occurred some 140 nautical miles away from the Ukrainian coast. A search has been launched for the missing crew and for any signs of an environmental threat. Radev warns of risk of widening conflict A maritime security source said initial assessments of the strike suggested it had probably been a Russian attack. Radev did not say who was behind the attack but made a reference to Russia's war in Ukraine. "If this war is not brought to an end in time, it will continue to expand its geographical scope and increase the risk of even a global conflict," he said. "We are seeing the war intensify, with all the rules of international law now being violated, and civilian vessels being attacked at sea. This is absolutely unacceptable." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also condemned the attack, saying: "Commercial ships — and innocent crews — are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea." Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X that Russia "makes navigation a challenge. By making navigation a challenge, it drives up risks, insurance and transport costs, and threatens the flow of food to global markets". Distress signals reported British maritime risk management group Vanguard said the attacks on Tuesday were on the Togo-flagged general cargo vessel ALFA WATAN and the Palau-flagged general cargo vessel ABLE, within Bulgaria's economic zone. The drone attack follows an incident in which Romanian authorities said on Monday two people had died in a fire on a ship in the Black Sea outside Romania's territorial waters. "The attacks represent a significant escalation in the threat to commercial shipping in the western Black Sea," maritime security firm MARISKS said in an advisory in which it advised captains and operators to watch out for drone activity in the area. "Of particular concern is the apparent geographic expansion of incidents beyond waters immediately adjacent to Ukraine and into the EEZs of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria." Zelenskiy blamed Russian drones for the Romania incident. Russian authorities have also made no comment on that incident. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, European countries have reported Russian drones breaching ⁠their ​airspace multiple times and mines floating in the ​Black Sea across trade and energy routes. https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/10/13/hunga.text: Hungarian former Prime Minister Viktor Orban has denied directing authorities to seize two Ukrainian cash-in-transit vehicles carrying $82 million in cash and gold, dismissing the claims as politically motivated. Seven Ukrainians transporting the assets were briefly detained by Hungarian authorities in March on suspicion of money laundering. The case increased tensions between Hungary and Ukraine before an April election that ended Russia ally Orban’s 16-year tenure as prime minister. Ukraine’s Oschadbank said its employees, transporting the cash and gold from Austria to Ukraine, had been engaged in a routine operation of the kind that it had ​carried out weekly since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Hungarian prosecutors launched an investigation into the handling of the case, including allegations of unlawful detention and mistreatment of the Ukrainian nationals. In June, prosecutors named Janos Hajdu, a former head of Hungary’s counter-terrorism forces and now security chief for Orban’s Fidesz party, as a suspect. Orban has not been questioned, but politicians from the governing Tisza party had challenged him to say whether he was involved. “Viktor Orban! Face the Hungarian people and say it clearly, directly, and in a manner worthy of a true leader: Did you give the order to stop the ‘gold convoy’, or not?” Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi wrote in a statement last week. On Monday, Orban called the transit of Ukrainian cash and gold “Europe’s biggest corruption case.” “I did not have to make specific decisions and order measures because, fortunately, the Hungarian authorities did their job of their own accord. But I would have done so anyway if they had not done it themselves,” Orban told Hir TV channel. “Now they want to bring me to court for this? … This has nothing to do with corruption, nothing to do with abuse of power. This is about wanting to eliminate the right wing.”
